lane.name: Barroom storytellers and deadpan songwriters
lane.definition: Wordy, funny-sad songwriting in the John Prine / David Berman line: half-spoken vocals, long verses, jokes that turn into grief, bar-band or home-studio backing.

albums.label: Orindal Records
albums.description: Owen Ashworth's post-Casiotone project sets deadpan, plainly sung short stories about Michigan, Christmas and lost people over minimal drum machine and synth. The songs are small and exact, with the quiet electronics leaving the narratives in front.
albums.lineage: Carries the deadpan storytelling of the Drag City school (Silver Jews) into Ashworth's own Orindal Records orbit, following directly from his Casiotone for the Painfully Alone records.

albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: The former Pearls and Brass drummer's third album drapes his cavernous, deadpan baritone over sampled loops and drum machines rather than a bar band. Its storytelling core of plainspoken, dark, small-town character studies fits the same funny-sad lineage as his songwriting peers.
albums.lineage: Follows All Hell (2012) and Me Moan (2013), both pre-2014 and outside this lane's window; Carnation extends his baritone-narrator style into a more electronic production.

albums.label: Sophomore Lounge
albums.description: A punked-up country record steeped in Louisville's weird, unassuming rock scene, with fiddle and banjo scrapping against fuzzy guitars behind Ryan Davis's character sketches of postmasters, coroners and drinkers. It sounds close to Souled American and Palace Brothers, rough and funny.
albums.lineage: Early-period State Champion, before Davis's Roadhouse Band turn; sounds indebted to the Drag City/Palace lineage that runs to Silver Jews and Purple Mountains.

albums.label: ATO Records
albums.description: Fritz folds synths and drum samples into his unconventional, wisecracking country songwriting, moving past the straighter honky-tonk of Dad Country toward a more hopeful, idiosyncratic sound. Titles like 'Chihuahua Rescue' signal the deadpan comic streak underneath.
albums.lineage: Follows Dad Country (2013); as Jonny Corndawg-turned-Fritz's later work, it sits at the more experimental, funny-sad end of the outlaw-adjacent Nashville scene.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Poole's self-released debut, a bedroom-recorded set built from drum machines and synthesizers under twangy vocal melodies, already showing the wry, deadpan lyric style he'd sharpen on later records. Rougher and more lo-fi than what followed, it is a deep cut for fans who want the beginning of the story.
albums.lineage: The starting point for Poole's country-by-way-of-DIY-indie sound that would develop through The Freelancer's Blues and The Rainbow Wheel of Death.
key_tracks: Don't You Think I'm Funny Anymore?

albums.label: Sophomore Lounge
albums.description: Ryan Davis's main band before his Roadhouse records: loose, twangy full-band arrangements built to carry his dense, surrealist wordplay. Send Flowers is their most fully realized record, with fiddle and ragged guitars under long, funny-sad verses. It sounds like a missing link between Silver Jews and the current Louisville deadpan-songwriter scene.
albums.lineage: Direct predecessor to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band through Davis himself; sounds rooted in the Drag City deadpan lineage.

albums.label: Seal Mountain Records
albums.description: A scrappy pop-punk and emo-pop record with late-'90s-indebted alt-rock energy. It is much more hook-driven and busy than the noise-country of the atlas core, with fast tempos and crowded arrangements.
albums.lineage: Sounds rooted in scrappier punk and emo rather than the storytelling style of the countrygaze bands.

albums.label: Wharf Cat Records
albums.description: Poole's second LP graduates from bedroom drum-machine country to a full honky-tonk band with wailing pedal steel. It updates classic countrypolitan storytelling for a young, broke, romantically alienated urban narrator, sung in his dry baritone.
albums.lineage: Follows his debut Wideass Highway; sounds like Haggard/Nelson/Kristofferson-style storytelling country moved into an ironic, digital-age idiom.

albums.label: Drag City
albums.description: David Berman's only album after retiring Silver Jews a decade earlier, made with members of Woods as his backing band, is his most bluntly autobiographical record, its jokes about divorce, depression and aging landing harder for being sung in the same flat, wry voice as ever. Berman died less than a month after its release, days before a scheduled tour, which makes songs like 'All My Happiness Is Gone' retroactively devastating. It stands as the culmination of his songwriting and a touchstone for the deadpan storytellers of this lane.
albums.lineage: David Berman's return after Silver Jews, rooted entirely in the Drag City deadpan lineage that runs from Starlite Walker through this final album.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Halper's debut mixes wry self-reflection with intricate fingerpicked instrumentals. Its title, Yiddish slang for a crass nouveau-riche success story, sets up the self-deprecating tone he'd carry into Schlemiel.
albums.lineage: Debut predecessor to Schlemiel; sounds indebted to Elliott Smith and fingerstyle players like Leo Kottke and William Tyler.

albums.label: Oh Boy Records
albums.description: Tre Burt's debut sets talky, literary verses over lo-fi fingerpicked guitar and rootsy production, favoring character sketches and slow-building narrative over hooks. It was independently released in 2019 before John Prine himself signed Burt to Oh Boy Records for its wider 2020 release. It plays like a front-porch reading more than a rock show, aimed at listeners who want the Prine lineage of plainspoken, half-sung storytelling.
albums.lineage: Directly anointed by John Prine, who signed Burt to his own Oh Boy Records, tying Burt's storytelling explicitly to the Prine/Tom T. Hall deadpan tradition that feeds the modern barroom-storyteller scene.

albums.label: Orindal Records
albums.description: Friendship frontman Dan Wriggins' solo debut strips his prose-poem lyrics down to quiet drums, classical guitar, and a big melodic organ, letting a wounded, deadpan voice turn diary-plain lines into gutting little jokes. Produced by bandmate Michael Cormier, it is five songs of fragmentary memory and small-town Maine imagery delivered with total seriousness despite the title. It works as a quieter, more confessional companion to Friendship's barroom rock.
albums.lineage: Extends the Philadelphia Friendship/Orindal circle's plainspoken, half-spoken songwriting, itself indebted to the Drag City deadpan school of Silver Jews and Smog that runs through the whole 2020s barroom-storyteller scene.

albums.label: Oh Boy Records
albums.description: Burt's second album narrates a cast of invented heroes and villains with a poet's eye for detail, closer to short fiction than confession. Fuller band arrangements surround his plainspoken, slightly raspy delivery without softening it, for listeners who want storytelling folk with some groove.
albums.lineage: Released on John Prine's Oh Boy Records, keeping Burt's storytelling tied to his mentor Prine and the plainspoken folk tradition he represents.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A live set cut at Levon Helm Studios, revisiting Made In America highlights in a stripped, in-the-room performance. Goodall's rolling piano and wry vocals come across warm and direct, with the room sound left in.
albums.lineage: Live companion to Made In America, recorded shortly after that LP's release.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: The ex-Ona keyboardist's debut swaps that band's rock for piano-man virtuosity and Zevon-ish snark. It is funny without playing as a comedy record, closer to plainspoken confession set to rolling piano.
albums.lineage: Follows Goodall's time in Ona; sounds indebted to the Randy Newman/Warren Zevon line of wry piano storytelling.

albums.label: Ruination Record Co.
albums.description: A piano-led, songs-first country record from the Fust bassist and Dear Life Records co-owner, mixing Neil Young-style keyboard balladry with Lambchop-esque narrative turns and field-recording interludes.
albums.lineage: Meadows co-runs Dear Life Records and plays in Fust, linking this solo record directly to that North Carolina/Brooklyn alt-country network.

albums.label: Mama Bird Recording Co.
albums.description: Smart, unfussy, mildly twangy folk built around dry, plainspoken wit about small-town Montana life. It sounds as gentle as Bahamas or Andy Shauf, but the lyrics carry the same funny-sad economy as his barroom-storyteller peers.
albums.lineage: Missoula, Montana songwriter whose work sits at the folk/country-adjacent end of the deadpan-storyteller lineage.

albums.label: Ruination Records
albums.description: Miller's debut full-length: hushed, homespun songwriting set against tape-hiss production and found-sound experiments. Pump organ, dulcimer-like textures and quiet guitar give it a front-porch, family-archive feel.
albums.lineage: Predates Losin'; sounds close to the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.

albums.label: Wharf Cat Records
albums.description: Poole's third solo LP pairs his golden, deadpan baritone with a live band plus old-school synthesizers, widening his millennial-malaise persona into songs about mortality and time rather than just dead-end jobs. The title track, named for the Mac beachball icon, is eerie and gently funny.
albums.lineage: Poole's country songwriting sounds descended from Haggard/Nelson/Kristofferson filtered through Brooklyn's DIY scene; the drum-machine-plus-pedal-steel sound recalls Silver Jews.

albums.label: Black Mountain // Soundly Music
albums.description: Bradshaw's character-driven songwriting captures life split between the north Georgia mountains and the touring road, recorded in five live days at Fellowship Hall Sound. Reviewers place him alongside Jason Isbell for narrative-driven, plainspoken Southern songwriting shot through with dry humor.
albums.lineage: Follows his 2021 LP Calico Jim, cut at the same Little Rock studio; part of a loose north-Georgia Appalachian storytelling trilogy completed by Thus Spoke the Fool.

albums.label: Sophomore Lounge
albums.description: Davis's first billed Roadhouse Band record: a double-LP set of long, expansive songs that mix folk-rooted wordplay with synth textures, organ swells and pedal steel. The mood is melancholic and gentle rather than rowdy. A good entry point for the barfly-poet strain of the scene before New Threats from the Soul refined it further.
albums.lineage: Follows Davis's work fronting State Champion; sounds indebted to Souled American, David Berman and Neil Young.

albums.label: Dear Life Records
albums.description: A compilation of Aaron Dowdy's early home-recorded songs, released as a single sprawling document of the years before Fust became a full band. Rough, home-taped country songs with Dowdy's drawl up front show the roots of the band's later, fuller storytelling. It is for fans who want to hear the sketches behind the band records.
albums.lineage: Predates and directly seeds the full-band Fust sound heard on Genevieve and Big Ugly; a look at the songwriter's home-recording origins before the Dear Life Records band era.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A sprawling album that gathers Jesse Welles' viral topical folk songs into a full deadpan-protest record, delivered in a flat, half-amused talk-sing that turns the grimmest subjects into wry asides. Built mostly on acoustic guitar and harmonica, it sounds like a modern update of Woody Guthrie topical folk filtered through Prine's dry humor. It suits listeners who want current-events songwriting that jokes its way toward grief rather than shouting.
albums.lineage: Sounds like a revival of the Guthrie/Prine topical-folk lineage for the social-media era, reaching listeners through viral video rather than the club circuit.

albums.label: Black Mountain Music / Soundly Music
albums.description: Bradshaw's character-driven historical songwriting, humanizing north-Georgia history and working-class locals. His rough, drawled voice sits over sparse, Appalachian-rooted arrangements.
albums.lineage: Follows Calico Jim and North Georgia Rounder in his run of north-Georgia story records.

albums.label: Sophomore Lounge
albums.description: Three Nashville songwriters trading instruments and lead vocals on an easygoing patio album with shaggy-dog charm. Feelies-ish jangle and Little Feat-style tempo shifts run through their group songwriting.
albums.lineage: Sounds close to the Nashville dive-bar scene of Lambchop and Silver Jews, and to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.

albums.label: Mtn Laurel Recording Co.
albums.description: A bittersweet, sharpened set of folk-rock songs full of shared-memory and loss storytelling drawn from his Asheville circle. Miller's plainspoken, half-sung delivery and homespun production put the focus on the writing over any studio polish.
albums.lineage: Follows Miller's debut Haw Creek; sounds of a piece with the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A cellist-songwriter's wry, meticulously detailed record, pairing relaxed, lush chamber-pop arrangements (cello interludes throughout) with DIY-punk detours and dryly funny lyrics. Closer to bedroom chamber-folk than a bar band, but its joke-then-gut-punch songwriting places it near the deadpan storyteller lineage.
albums.lineage: A borderline Core inclusion: less bar-band than her C2 peers, but shares the funny-sad lyrical mode with Prine/Berman-style songwriters.

albums.label: Gar Hole Records
albums.description: Fritz's return after a long break turns blue-collar everyday life into wry, anthemic country songs. Honky-tonk band arrangements back his nasal, joke-laced delivery, with the humor always edging toward sadness.
albums.lineage: Follows Sweet Creep (2016) after a near-decade recording gap; continues his idiosyncratic, joke-laced country songwriting.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A keys-heavy, conversational sophomore album about relationships, mixing fingerpicked folk, indie rock and pop confessionals. The Yiddish title signals the same rueful, self-deprecating humor that runs through his songwriting.
albums.lineage: Follows Halper's 2020 debut Alrightnik; a Nashville songwriter working the same wry, wordy vein as his singer-songwriter peers.

albums.label: Drag City
albums.description: Mess Esque is Helen Franzmann (McKisko) and Mick Turner (Dirty Three), and this is a twisted, handmade folk record that builds a warm, dreamlike world out of plainspoken vocals and loose, unhurried arrangements. Turner's shimmering guitar loops circle under Franzmann's voice. It sounds openhearted and slightly askew at once.
albums.lineage: Released on Drag City alongside Bill Callahan and Bonnie 'Prince' Billy, placing Mess Esque within that label's wry, left-of-center songwriting world.

albums.label: Memorials of Distinction / Dog Day Records
albums.description: Mildred's debut EP introduces the four-singer, four-songwriter format they'd expand on Fenceline. It is homemade and intimate, with trading lead vocals over living-room-scale guitar arrangements.
albums.lineage: Precedes Fenceline as the band's first release.

albums.album: I'm Sad as Hell and I'm Not Going to Fake It Anymore
albums.label: Sipsman
albums.description: Janky, livewire guitars and winking humor meet surprisingly massive choruses, somewhere between Amen Dunes and a Lou Reed doing country. The title alone sets the funny-sad tone that carries through songs about content-creation anxiety and modern malaise.
albums.lineage: Sounds close to the Northeast indie-twang of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird; extends jokey, confessional indie-folk songwriting into anthemic rock territory.

albums.label: Sophomore Lounge
albums.description: A sprawling seven-song double LP of conversational barfly rock, Davis half-sings dense, punning verses over a loose Roadhouse Band arrangement that folds pedal steel and violin into synths and programmed beats. It is dark, funny and grand at once, with guest harmonies from Will Oldham, Catherine Irwin and Lou Turner deepening its Drag City-indebted, David Berman-adjacent lineage. For listeners who want the modern high-water mark of wordy, tragicomic songwriting.
albums.lineage: Davis fronted the earlier Louisville band State Champion before going solo with the Roadhouse Band; the record extends the Silver Jews/David Berman line of deadpan storytelling into the 2020s.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A piano-driven, introspective record about returning to his West Virginia hometown, with the sophisticated melodic sense of Made In America turned toward homesickness rather than jokes. It rounds out Goodall's small catalog of plainspoken, piano-led songwriting.
albums.lineage: Follows Made In America and a Levon Helm Studios live set; continues his piano-based storytelling, which sounds indebted to Zevon and Newman.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Gibson's fourth full-length, a slow-building record of Florida noir vignettes that trades his earlier sample-collage approach for a more spacious, bar-at-closing-time mood. His deep, deadpan baritone carries Southern gothic storytelling over sparse arrangements.
albums.lineage: Fourth Daughn Gibson LP, following Carnation (2015); continues his deadpan-narrator persona in a stripped-down mode.

albums.label: Memorials of Distinction / Dog Day Records
albums.description: The Oakland quartet's breezy, affecting debut LP, with four singers and songwriters trading lead vocals from laconic to full-throated. Conversational lyrics and a living-room-session intimacy carry its funny-sad, plainspoken storytelling.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the funny-sad, plainspoken songwriting in the barroom-storyteller lane.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: The trio's follow-up to Real Time leans further into playful genre-hopping, with lounge, B-52's pulse and Glen Campbell dust. It keeps the same trading-instruments, trading-verses songwriting method.
albums.lineage: Sounds close to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band and MJ Lenderman and the Wind.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: London songwriter Michael Rea's charming, conversational folk-rock record moves at an ambling, unhurried pace, its plainspoken verses and breezy melodies squarely in the wordy funny-sad tradition despite its UK setting.
albums.lineage: A non-US example of the Prine/Berman deadpan-storyteller mode, showing the style's reach beyond its American scenes.

albums.label: Ruination Record Co.
albums.description: Sam Sodomsky's songwriting project sounds akin to David Berman, John Darnielle and Dan Bejar: clever, plainspoken songs balancing folksy earnestness against wry self-awareness. Gentle guitar arrangements leave room for the lyrics to do the work. It suits listeners who come to songs for the words.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to the deadpan-songwriter lineage of Berman and Darnielle, within the small Brooklyn Ruination Record Co. circle.
key_tracks: To Everything There Is A Ceiling
